title: Inline styles per element vs one shared class
variable: identical inline declarations per element vs a shared class
claim: Antipattern #29 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: 'inline styles per element for shared looks - defeats rule sharing, bloats style data.' This is the STATIC form of the question: not whether writing styles per frame is expensive (style-write-scope covers that), but whether a page that simply holds N identical inline declarations carries a standing cost against one that shares a class. It matters for anything generated by a component framework, which routinely inlines what could have been a class.
result: NOT CONFIRMED. No reliable difference at 30, 100 or 300 elements on any phase. Holding N identical inline declarations costs nothing measurable against sharing one class, so the web claim about defeating rule sharing and bloating style data does not reproduce here as a per-frame cost. Together with style-write-scope - where inline writes were the CHEAPER way to invalidate many elements - the lab finds no per-frame case against inline styles in Gameface. This measures steady-state cost only; it says nothing about memory or about maintainability, which remain the real arguments for classes.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. Rule 1: one variable, where the shared declarations live. Rule 2: identical DOM, same element count, same geometry, same rendered appearance - the inline declarations are byte-equivalent to the .shared rule. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_INLINE constant; both pages define both paths and both set left/top inline, so inline-style machinery is exercised in A too and only the three shared declarations move. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: static page plus the shared root-nudge damage driver - deliberately no churn, because the standing cost is the question. Rule 7: no randomness. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Styles. NOTE: both pages carry the .shared rule in the stylesheet even though B never matches it, so the stylesheets are byte-identical and rule count cannot leak into the comparison.
